worksheet.title: The Wrong Direction
worksheet.subtitle: A move goes the wrong way — fix it
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find a move that goes the wrong way and fix its direction.

parts.title: The goal: both reach 2
parts.text: Bit (green) and Pixel (purple) both start on the green flag. They should BOTH reach number 2. One script is correct, but the other has a move going the WRONG WAY — forward when it should go back. Read both, find the wrong direction, and fix it.

parts.title: Run both
parts.prompt: Where does each land? Bit (home 0, forward 2): ____  Pixel (home 4, forward 2): ____. (Remember: a sprite cannot go past 5.) Which one misses the goal 2?

parts.title: Find the wrong direction
parts.prompt: Pixel starts at 4 and needs to reach 2. Is 2 in FRONT of Pixel or BEHIND it? So which way should Pixel move — forward or back?

parts.title: Fix it
parts.prompt: Write Pixel's fixed move: ____ 2 (forward or back?). After the fix, where does Pixel land? Do both reach the goal now?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A move can have the right number but the wrong DIRECTION. Look at where the sprite starts and where the goal is: if the goal is behind it, the move must go back, not forward. Here Pixel needed back 2, not forward 2.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 2 · Debugging & Reading Code
teacher_guide.title: The Wrong Direction
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students fix a wrong-direction bug. The goal is for both to reach 2; Bit is right, but Pixel moves forward (away from 2) when it should move back. Students reason about which way the goal is. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer needed — paper and a pencil. You read the prompts aloud. Optional: two counters on a number line 0 to 5 (green Bit, purple Pixel) so children can trace both sets of moves and see which one misses the goal.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Is the goal in front of Pixel or behind it? That tells you forward or back.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — Bit reaches 2; Pixel goes forward to 5 (overshoots).
3. Let them try. Students decide the direction and write the fix (Ex 2–3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Bit: 0, forward 2 → 2 (reaches goal). Pixel: 4, forward 2 → 5 (the path stops at 5; Pixel overshoots and misses 2).
Exercise 2 — the goal 2 is behind Pixel (Pixel is at 4), so Pixel should move back, not forward.
Exercise 3 — fixed move back 2 → Pixel lands on 2. Both reach 2. The number (2) was fine; only the direction changes.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: changing the number instead of the direction. Here only the direction is wrong.
Make it easier: stand Pixel's counter on 4 and point toward the goal to find the direction.
Make it harder: ask what would happen if both the number and direction were wrong.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
In plain terms: students write and run instructions, including two sets that run at the same time.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read two sets of instructions, find and fix the wrong one, and explain the fix.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child flips Pixel's direction so it reaches the goal.
